frase_gancho.texto: A monkey of volcanic glass, polished until it becomes a mirror.

puente_narrativo.texto: From one animal that leaps and plays, we move on to another that also leaps. Look for an insect made of red stone, its legs ready to jump: it is the name of this forest written in stone.

guion_corto.texto: This black obsidian vessel is barely fourteen centimeters tall, yet it is one of the jewels of the museum. It represents a seated spider monkey, with arms and legs hugging the body of the container; the tail curves over the back and forms the opening. Obsidian is volcanic glass: it shatters with a sharp blow, and working it into this shape without breaking it was a remarkable feat. Notice the shine: the polish is so fine that it almost works as a mirror. For the Mexica, the monkey was associated with wind, dance, and play. The piece was found in Texcoco and came to the museum in the nineteenth century.

guion_largo.texto:
Before seeing how it was made, think about the material. Obsidian is volcanic glass, and you have already come across it on this tour: in the points of the first hunters, more than ten thousand years ago, and in the blades of Teotihuacán, finer than a scalpel. Here it reaches its fullest expression. After thousands of years of use, it is no longer a tool: it is sculpture.

Carving a vessel from obsidian is madness. The material fractures with a sharp blow and forgives no mistakes. The lapidaries had to wear it down and polish it with fine sand and water, perhaps for months, and without any blows. A single error could ruin weeks of work. That this piece has arrived intact, after some five centuries, is almost a miracle.

Why a monkey? For the Mexica, the monkey, ozomatli, was an animal of restless energy: it leaps, spins, dances. It was the sign of a day in the ritual calendar related to festivity, play, and the arts, the domain of [Xochipilli](mna_s06_xochipilli), the god you have just seen. It was also linked with the wind, and with Ehécatl-Quetzalcóatl, the god with the bird-beak mask that you already know. It was said that the wind swept the road clear for the rains, and the monkey, which is never still, was a fitting image of that wind.

There is something more. Spider monkeys do not live on the high plateau; they live in warm jungles, far from Texcoco. The Mexica probably knew them as animals brought from the south, like quetzal feathers and cacao: another product of an empire that received things from very far away. Sculpting it in the most difficult material to work was a way of saying that whoever owned it could have the rarest of things.

Look at its rounded belly. Some read it as a pregnant female, an image of fertility. That is an interpretation, not a certainty. What is certain is the care: the bent arms, the short legs, the face with wrinkles around the half-open mouth, as if it were about to let out a cry or a puff of breath. It seems alive inside the crystal.

What was it used for? We do not know exactly. It is thought to have been a luxury container, perhaps for keeping valuable or ritual substances, and that it belonged to an elite. What is certain is that it was not a kitchen object.

Its modern history sounds like a tale. It is said that a farmer found it near Texcoco and traded it for a sheep to a patient of the physician Rafael Lucio; and that in 1869 the doctor handed it over to the National Museum in exchange for a diamond ring. The anecdote was recorded by Eugène Boban, an antiquarian from the time of Maximilian, so it should be taken with caution. What is certain is that it came to the museum in the nineteenth century.

See how the light enters the black stone. Obsidian was also the material of the divination mirrors of the god Tezcatlipoca, “Smoking Mirror,” the same one from the legend of the mirror that you already know. A monkey and a mirror: two ways for the world to look at itself.

texto.Dimensions: 14 cm high x 15 cm wide x 16.5 cm thick

texto.pregunta: Myth: Spider monkeys were common animals in the Valley of Mexico.
texto.respuesta: Reality: They live in warm jungles in the south, far from the high plateau. An obsidian monkey was a luxury object from remote places.
